The best 3-qubit chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I picked it using garnet's current default calibration (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). Its two IRB CZ fidelities are 0.99802 for QB12-QB7 and 0.99869 for QB12-QB11. Their product is 0.99671. That is the highest product of any connected chain on the chip. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, at 0.99469.

I then ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits on garnet:mock with 200 shots. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal superposition of 0 and 1. It then copies that state onto QB7 and onto QB11, using one CZ gate on each of the pairs QB12-QB7 and QB12-QB11 plus single-qubit rotations. It measures all 3 qubits. The job ID is 01a160a4-0f93-7289-931e-a0f48abf1a43. I read the circuit back from the server. It has 2 CZ gates, both on the chosen pairs, and it measures QB7, QB12 and QB11.

The counts, in the order QB7 QB12 QB11, were 000: 54, 001: 51, 110: 53 and 111: 42. A perfect quantum computer would give only 000 and 111, each about half the time. A noiseless simulation of the exact circuit I sent confirms this 50/50 split. The mock backend does not run the circuit. It returns random placeholder results, so these counts tell you nothing about the physics. The mock run cost 0 credits.

The principle is entanglement. In a GHZ state all 3 qubits share one joint state. Each qubit on its own reads 0 or 1 at random. But on a real device the 3 readings should agree almost every time. Choosing the qubit pairs with the best measured CZ fidelity gives that agreement the best chance to survive the device's noise. To see the real effect, the same circuit would need to run on real garnet, which costs credits.
